comments.author: saraathotkey
comments.content:
The audience question is an important one - how can we capture mainstream interest? And whoever cracks that one will win the game! We've tried the "being useful" route with pushing our interactive iBook of Maggot Moon to schools as a teaching tool - with only very slow progress. 
Basically, people don't know what it is or how they can use it until we can sit down one on one with them and show it to them, get it in their hands to play with. Then, they are amazed and on board. 
Interestingly, this reminds me of my experience with video games as a teen girl. If someone would show me the basics, (say of Final Fantasy) I would obsess for hours trying to breed the right chocobo, but a game I had to figure out completely on my own left me baffled and not bothered.

comments.author: Stephen Hart
comments.content:
Thanks for the post Alex. I think there is a lot of potential in the schools, maybe some form of competition for creating content, best entry gets published or added to a compendium. The idea of leaving an experience in the story as you go for others to 'find' sounds brilliant, but tricky to implement.

I have also been intrigued at the amount of 'fan' content that has been generated around the Star Wars franchise, a solid main theme that has some openness can entice people to fill in the gaps or build a whole new back story for specific events.
